title: Globalisation and Trade
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the invisible threads connecting your daily life to factories and farms around the world -- and the fierce debate over who wins and who loses from globalisation.
competenceGoals: analyze causes and consequences of globalisation

content.content:
## The world in your pocket

Take out your phone and think about its journey. Designed in one country, with minerals mined in several others, components made in still more, assembled somewhere else, and sold to you through a global network -- that single object is a map of **globalisation**, the increasing interconnectedness of the world's economies, cultures and populations. The clothes you wear, the food you eat, the music you stream all reflect a world where borders have become increasingly porous, with international trade as the economic engine driving it.

This matters because globalisation shapes employment, wages and opportunities in every country, and Norway -- a small, open economy -- is deeply woven into the global trading system. The debates about globalisation, over who benefits and who loses, sit at the centre of modern politics. To follow them, you need to understand what drives globalisation, why countries trade at all, and the long-running argument between free trade and protectionism.

## What drives it, and why countries trade

Globalisation is propelled by several forces working together. **Technological drivers** include the internet and digital communication enabling instant connectivity, container shipping that slashed transport costs since the 1960s, cheaper air travel, and automation that lets companies coordinate complex supply chains. **Economic drivers** include the reduction of trade barriers through international agreements, institutions like the World Trade Organization, the IMF and the World Bank, the deregulation of financial markets, and the rise of multinational corporations operating across many countries. **Political drivers** include the end of the Cold War in 1991 opening new markets, and regional trade agreements like the EU, USMCA and ASEAN. **Cultural drivers** include global media, English as a common language, and migration creating cultural bridges. Globalisation thus operates across economic, political, cultural and technological dimensions at once.

But why do countries trade in the first place? The classic answer is **comparative advantage**, a theory developed by David Ricardo in 1817. Its insight is subtle and powerful: even if one country can produce *everything* more efficiently than another, both countries still benefit if each specialises in what it produces *relatively* most efficiently and trades for the rest. This is the bedrock of the argument for free trade. Picture a smartphone's global journey -- minerals from one continent, design from another, assembly in a third -- as comparative advantage in action, each region contributing what it does relatively best. The theory explains why trade can, in principle, make everyone better off. Whether it actually does, and who shares in the gains, is exactly where the debate begins.

content.content:
## Free trade versus protectionism: a balanced look

One of the oldest debates in economics is how far governments should regulate international trade, and a fair treatment lays out both sides. **Free trade** is the principle that goods and services should flow across borders without government interference. Its supporters argue it brings lower prices through competition, greater variety, efficiency via comparative advantage, economic growth and innovation, and even international cooperation that reduces conflict. **Protectionism**, by contrast, uses government policies to restrict imports and protect domestic industries. Its common tools are *tariffs* (taxes on imports), *quotas* (limits on quantities), *subsidies* (payments to domestic producers), and *non-tariff barriers* (regulations that make foreign goods harder to sell). Its supporters argue it protects domestic jobs, shields "infant industries" not yet competitive, ensures national security through domestic production, prevents "dumping" (selling below cost to destroy competitors), and can protect environmental and labour standards. Neither position is simply right -- each reflects real values and real costs.

The **World Trade Organization**, established in 1995 as successor to GATT, provides the rules-based framework that tries to manage these tensions. Its core principles include Most-Favoured-Nation treatment (benefits given to one member extend to all), National Treatment (imported goods treated equally to domestic ones once inside the market), and transparency. Yet the WTO faces growing strain from trade wars and geopolitical rivalry. Norway's place in this system is distinctive: it is *not* an EU member, but participates in the European Economic Area through the EFTA agreement, giving it access to the EU single market. Its main exports are petroleum, seafood, metals and maritime services, and its economy is heavily dependent on international trade -- a vivid reminder that for a small, open country, the outcome of these global debates is not abstract at all.

questions.task: Which is a common protectionist tool?

options.text: A tariff -- a tax on imported goods

questions.solution: Tariffs (taxes on imports), along with quotas, subsidies and non-tariff barriers, are common protectionist tools used to restrict imports.

questions.task: Which is an argument FOR free trade?

options.text: It lowers prices through competition and increases variety
It shields domestic jobs from all competition

questions.solution: Supporters of free trade point to lower prices, greater variety, efficiency and growth; the other options are arguments for protectionism.

questions.task: How is Norway connected to the EU single market without being a member?

options.text: Through the European Economic Area via the EFTA agreement
It has no access at all

questions.solution: Norway is not an EU member but participates in the European Economic Area through EFTA, giving it access to the EU single market.

questions.task: Why does the chapter present both free trade and protectionism fairly?

options.text: Because each reflects real values and real costs

questions.solution: The chapter notes that neither position is simply right -- free trade and protectionism each reflect genuine values and trade-offs, so both deserve a balanced hearing.

content.content:
## In short

Globalisation -- the deepening interconnectedness of economies, cultures and populations -- is driven by technology, trade liberalisation, political change and cultural exchange, and operates across multiple dimensions at once. The theory of comparative advantage explains why countries benefit from specialising and trading, even when one is more efficient at everything. The enduring debate between free trade and protectionism has fair arguments on both sides: free trade promises lower prices and growth but can harm vulnerable workers and industries, while protectionism shields jobs and standards but can raise prices and reduce efficiency. The WTO provides the rules of the game, though it faces mounting pressure, and Norway -- a small, open economy tied to the EU single market through the EEA -- shows how much these global debates matter to ordinary lives.
